name: Natural killer cell deficiency
aliases: classical and functional NK cell deficiency

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: Natural killer cell deficiency is a rare primary immunodeficiency defined by absent or dysfunctional NK cells with otherwise preserved lymphocyte lineages
It is subdivided into classical deficiency (NK cells are absent or greatly reduced) and functional deficiency (NK cells are present but cannot perform cytotoxicity)
The characteristic infection susceptibility is to severe herpesvirus infections, including herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus
Severe or recurrent herpesvirus disease, sometimes disseminated or life-threatening, in the absence of another obvious immunodeficiency should raise suspicion
Human papillomavirus-related disease can also be prominent in some forms
Reported genetic causes include mutations affecting GATA2, MCM4, and other genes important for NK cell development or function
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating absent NK cells or impaired NK cytotoxic function after excluding secondary causes and other primary immunodeficiencies
Management centres on antiviral prophylaxis and prompt antiviral treatment, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in severe forms such as GATA2 deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that provide early defence against virally infected and transformed cells through cytotoxic granule release and cytokine production, and they are particularly important in controlling herpesviruses. In classical NK cell deficiency, mutations disrupt the development or survival of the NK lineage, so few or no NK cells are present; in functional deficiency, NK cells develop but cannot kill their targets because of defects in cytotoxic machinery or activating signals. The loss of this early antiviral surveillance leaves patients unable to contain herpesvirus infections, which can become severe or disseminated. Some causative genes, such as GATA2, also affect broader haematopoiesis, producing additional cytopenias and predisposition to myeloid malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Combined immunodeficiencies affecting T-cell antiviral immunity
GATA2 deficiency (as a broader bone marrow failure and immunodeficiency syndrome)
HIV and other causes of acquired immunodeficiency
Chediak-Higashi syndrome and other disorders of cytotoxic granules
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subset analysis quantifying NK cells (CD3-negative, CD56/CD16-positive)
Genetic testing (including GATA2, MCM4 and related genes)
Full blood count and bone marrow evaluation where GATA2 deficiency is suspected
Viral studies for herpesviruses during acute infection
Exclusion of secondary causes of low or impaired NK cells
redFlags: Severe, disseminated, or recurrent herpesvirus infection requiring urgent antiviral therapy and immunological workup
Progressive cytopenias or evolving myeloid malignancy in GATA2-associated disease
Live vaccines should be approached with caution given impaired antiviral immunity
Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in functional cytotoxicity defects
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with the specific defect and the severity of viral disease; isolated functional deficiencies may be managed with antiviral strategies, whereas broader defects such as GATA2 deficiency carry risks of bone marrow failure and malignancy and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
pitfalls: Attributing severe herpesvirus infections to bad luck rather than investigating NK cell function
Relying on NK cell numbers alone and missing a functional deficiency with normal counts
Failing to recognise GATA2 deficiency as a cause with wider haematological consequences
Not excluding secondary causes of reduced NK cells before diagnosing a primary deficiency
Overlooking the need for antiviral prophylaxis
management: Treat herpesvirus infections promptly and aggressively with aciclovir or valaciclovir, and ganciclovir or valganciclovir for cytomegalovirus, given the characteristic susceptibility to severe herpesvirus disease
Use long-term antiviral prophylaxis to prevent recurrent or disseminated herpesvirus infection
Manage human papillomavirus-related disease with immunisation and ablative or topical treatment where prominent
In GATA2 deficiency, monitor blood counts and marrow and undertake surveillance for bone marrow failure and myeloid malignancy
Offer allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can be curative in severe classical deficiency and GATA2-related disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through clinical immunology and haematology and keep vaccinations up to date
Provide genetic counselling and family screening for the identified causative gene
